title: Which SOLID principles matter most in LLD: Single Responsibility (one class, one job), Open/Closed (extend behavior without modifying existing code), Liskov Substitution (child can replace parent), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concrete classes)?
shortTitle: Which SOLID principles matter most in LLD?
keyPoints: In day-to-day LLD, SRP, OCP, LSP, and DIP carry the most weight; ISP supports them.
SRP keeps each class focused on one reason to change, preventing merge conflicts and cross-concern bugs.
OCP lets you add new behaviour by adding a class, not editing tested code, reducing regression risk.
LSP ensures any implementation can drop into a service without special-case handling.
DIP makes services testable by depending on injected abstractions, not concrete classes.
SOLID is guidance, not dogma: applied mechanically it creates needless interfaces; applied with judgment it makes banking systems that evolve safely.

s1_definition.oneliner: In LLD, SRP keeps classes focused, OCP adds behaviour without edits, LSP guarantees substitutability, and DIP makes everything testable through injected abstractions.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **SOLID** is a set of five object-oriented design principles that produce loosely coupled, highly cohesive, and easily extensible code.
- **SRP (Single Responsibility)** – one class, one reason to change; prevents cross-concern bugs.
- **OCP (Open/Closed)** – extend by adding a class, not editing tested code; reduces regression risk.
- **LSP (Liskov Substitution)** – any subtype drops in without breaking callers; enables polymorphism.
- **DIP (Dependency Inversion)** – depend on abstractions, inject implementations; makes code testable.
- **ISP (Interface Segregation)** – keep interfaces small so classes are not forced to implement unused methods.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a well-run branch. Each employee does one job (SRP). To add a new service, you hire a new specialist rather than retraining everyone (OCP). Any trained teller can replace another without breaking the queue (LSP). And the manager gives instructions to a role like teller, not to a specific person named Rajesh, so anyone filling that role works (DIP).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  SOLID in an LLD Banking Module
  ──────────────────────────────

  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  InterestModule  │  (SRP: only calculates interest)
  │  ───────────     │
  │  - strategy map  │
  └────────┬────────┘
           │ DIP: depends on interface
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  InterestStrategy    │ ◄── interface (ISP: one method)
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ LSP: any impl drops in
     ┌───────┼───────┬───────────┐
     ▼       ▼       ▼           ▼
  Savings  Current   NRE      FixedDeposit
  (0.04)   (0.02)   (0.065)   (new – OCP)

  Adding FixedDeposit = new class
  InterestModule + existing strategies: UNTOUCHED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SOLID is five principles, and in real low-level design four of them do most of the heavy lifting. Single Responsibility means each class has exactly one reason to change, so Rajesh keeps interest calculation in an interest service and notifications in an alert service at National Bank of India, because a change to the SMS vendor should never risk breaking interest math.

Open/Closed means code is open for extension but closed for modification. When the bank launches a new deposit product, Pankaj adds a new strategy class implementing the interest interface rather than editing a growing if-else, so he never re-tests the existing, regulator-approved logic.

Liskov Substitution means any implementation must honour the contract, so wherever the service expects an interest strategy, any concrete strategy drops in and behaves correctly without special cases. Dependency Inversion means the high-level service depends on the strategy abstraction, not on a concrete class, which Rajesh wires through constructor injection, making the service trivial to unit test with a mock.

ISP keeps interfaces small so classes implement only what they need. The senior insight is that SOLID is judgment, not dogma: applied mechanically it breeds needless interfaces, but applied thoughtfully it lets the interest module absorb new products and regulatory changes without destabilising proven code.

Remember one sentence: in LLD, SRP focuses each class, OCP extends by adding, LSP guarantees substitutability, and DIP makes everything testable through injected abstractions.
